title: Go for No: The Counterintuitive Path to More Yeses
summary: Andrea Waltz co-founded Courage Crafters with her husband Richard Fenton and co-wrote Go for No!, the 80-page sales fable that has sold more than half a million copies, along with the follow-ups When They Say No and Go for No! The Sequel. Her argument is that most sellers optimize for hearing yes when the faster path to revenue is collecting no's on purpose: disqualify early, ask the hard question first, and stop spending months massaging deals that were never going to close. She walks through the two questions she uses to qualify her own speaking prospects, the difference between a good no and a no from someone who has no authority to say yes, and the five levels of failure that move a rep from tolerating rejection to actively seeking it. Listen if you are an account executive who cannot bring yourself to kill a weak opportunity, or a sales leader deciding what activity to reward.
keyQuote: You've got to completely change your philosophy and become a gatekeeper to your own products, services, whatever it is you're selling. The best way to do that is through disqualification.
guestBio: Andrea Waltz launched her own training company at 24 and built her early career in retail, the industry she and her husband Richard Fenton first sold speaking and training workshops into. The two co-founded Courage Crafters, Inc., now based in Central Florida, and co-wrote Go for No! Yes is the Destination, No is How You Get There, an 80-page fable that has sold more than half a million copies. They followed it with When They Say No, a guide to handling rejection in sales, and more recently with Go for No! The Sequel. Waltz keynotes and runs corporate training for financial services, insurance, retail, and direct sales organizations, and is a member of the National Speakers Association. She also runs 21-day Go for No challenges with small cohorts of eight to twelve sellers drawn from different industries.
takeaways: Disqualify first. Persuasion comes after, not before.
Be a gatekeeper to your own product, not a pitchman.
Ask what they want before you argue about what they need.
A no from someone who cannot say yes is not a real no.
Set no goals and celebrate the activity, not just the wins.
Nine years of follow-up is a normal cycle, not a failure.
Closed-lost fields lie. The call transcripts do not.
